doc.title: Stefon Harris interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 11, 2020

title: Audience question: how jazz improvisation works
summary: Harris likens improvising to speaking without words and says he works on ear and vocabulary toward not knowing.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: We have two more, they’re both about improv. Another one is how would you describe your process of improv? How does jazz improv work?
Well so much of jazz improvisation is directly connected to language for me. When I’m improvising I’m literally speaking in the exact same way that I’m speaking right now. I

just take the words away. So all the rhythms, all the nuances are here. The way that I speak is exactly the way that I play [scats]. I can take [scats] everything I say [scats] and play it on an instrument [scats]. Right? So the type of flow that I have when we’re communicating right now is the same type of flow that I want to have when I’m onstage. Now the challenge is we’re using language all the time and most of the time we’re more comfortable speaking than we are playing. The language of harmony is so — it’s not complex it’s just a lot. So I spend the majority of my time working on my ear and learning little tiny bits of vocabulary so that whatever it is I hear I can react to it. So the goal ultimately is to not know. Right? It’s like I almost want to forget everything that I’m learning and I hope that one day I can get to that and just say I don’t need to know what the song is, let’s just play. And you can just hear and react. I’m not there, I’ve got a long way to go, but that keeps me hungry. But again, at the center of great improvisation I still think it’s being able to understand that your idea comes to life relative to what’s happening around you. You can take a single note and you just go [gestures] right at the right moment and it’s just, man, the whole audience will start clapping. And it’s just like one note, it’s not even a special note, its placement and timing relative to everyone else.
